rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك وبريدة
rows.claim: Ibn Mardawayh reports that the Prophet identified these houses as prophets’ houses; when Abu Bakr asked about Ali and Fatima’s home, he said it was among the most excellent, a report al-Alusi says should stand if sound.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك وبريدة قال : قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan takes the houses generally to include mosques and homes where prayer and religious learning occur.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان : الظاهر أنها مطلقة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan also allows the houses to symbolize believers’ prayers or bodies, likened to mosques; al-Alusi finds this interpretation unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد بها صلاة المؤمنين أو أبدانهم بأن تشبه صلاتهم الجامعة للعبادات القولية والفعلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permission means God’s command, and raising the houses means honoring them; al-Alusi identifies this as the sound explanation of the phrase.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالإذن الأمر وبالرفع التعظيم أي أمر سبحانه بتعظيم قدرها وروي هذا عن الحسن والضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the houses are mosques, honoring them entails protecting them from ritual impurity and contamination: jurists prohibit entry by menstruating or postpartum women and the ritually impure, even in transit, and bar anything likely to soil them.
rows.anchor: إذا أريد بها المساجد فتعظيم قدرها يكون بأشياء شتى كصيانتها عن دخول الجنب والحائض والنفساء ولو على وجه العبور

rows.speaker: واثلة بن الأسقع
rows.claim: Ibn Majah transmits from Wathila that the Prophet instructed people to keep mosques free of children, the insane, commerce, disputes, loud voices, punishments, and drawn swords, and to provide water places and incense them on Fridays.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن ماجة عن واثلة بن الأسقع عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : جنبوا مساجدكم

rows.speaker: ثوبان
rows.claim: Thawban reports the Prophet’s instruction to rebuke people who recite poetry or announce lost property in mosques, repeating the prescribed rebuke three times.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج الطبراني وابن السني وابن منده عن ثوبان قال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on poetry applies to blameworthy verse, such as satire of Muslims or erotic and wine poetry; verse praising prophecy or Islam, imparting wisdom, or encouraging virtue and asceticism is allowed.
rows.anchor: وينبغي أن يقيد المنع من إنشاد الشعر بما إذا كان فيه شيء مذموم كهجو المسلم وصفة الخمر

rows.speaker: رجل من الأنصار
rows.claim: A Companion from the Ansar reports that anyone finding a louse in a mosque should wrap it in his garment and remove it after leaving.
rows.anchor: عن رجل من الأنصار قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : إذا وجد أحدكم القملة في المسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Discarding a killed louse in a mosque is mildly disliked, and a live one should not be left there; urinating there is forbidden even into a container.
rows.anchor: ومنع إلقاء القملة فيه بعد قتلها وهو مكروه تنزيها على ما صرح به بعض المتأخرين ويندب أن لا تلقى حية في المسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi has not found an explicit ruling on bloodletting into a container in a mosque, but says it should be treated like urination because both urine and blood are gravely impure.
rows.anchor: وفي الأشباه وأما الفصد في المسجد في إناء فلم أره وينبغي أن لا فرق أي لأن كلا من البول والدم نجس مغلظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spitting and bodily mucus must be kept out of mosques; ablution there is disliked as naturally repugnant, so mosques must be kept clean.
rows.anchor: وفي البدائع يكره التوضيء في المسجد لأنه مستقذر طبعا فيجب تنزيه المسجد عنه كما يجب تنزيهه عن المخاط والبلغم

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi reports that the Prophet scraped phlegm from the mosque’s qibla wall and applied perfume there, calling the act a Sunna; phlegm on top of a mat is less bad than underneath, and if unavoidable it should be buried.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي شيبة عن الشعبي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم رأى في قبلة المسجد نخامة فقام إليها فحكها بيده الشريفة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report from Anas says spitting in a mosque is a sin and its expiation is to cover it; al-Alusi adds that al-Tabarani transmits a similar report from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أخرجه ابن أبي شيبة عن أنس مرفوعا التفل في المسجد خطيئة وكفارته أن يواريه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sexual intercourse and relieving oneself in or atop a mosque are forbidden.
rows.anchor: ومنع الوطء فيها وفوقها كالتخلي وصرحوا بحرمة ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People with odor from garlic, onions, leeks, radishes, chronic bad breath, strong body odor, or foul-smelling clothes should not enter; garlic-smelling men were led to al-Baqiʿ in the Prophet’s time.
rows.anchor: ومنع دخول من أكل ذا رائحة كريهة فيها كالثوم والبصل والكراث وأكل الفجل إذا تجشا كذلك

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says oil-makers should stay back and not take the front rows, evidently because of their odor.
rows.anchor: وعن مالك أن الزياتين يتأخرون ولا يتقدمون أي إلى الوصف الأول ويقعدون في أخريات الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eating garlic in a mosque is prohibited for anyone not in retreat; sitting there for condolences or worldly conversation is prohibited, and using a mosque as a passage is disliked or forbidden.
rows.anchor: ومنع الثوم والأكل فيها لغير معتكف ومنع الجلوس فيها للمصيبة أو للتحدث بكلام الدنيا ومنع اتخاذها طريقا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Umar traces the prohibition on passing through mosques to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقد جار النهي عن ذلك في حديث رواه ابن ماجه عن ابن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما مرفوعا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that making a mosque a thoroughfare is one of the signs of the Hour; habitually doing so is sinful and makes a person publicly disobedient, while a genuine excuse removes the dislike.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي شيبة عن ابن مسعود أن اتخاذها طريقا من أشراط الساعة وفي القنية معتاد ذلك يأثم ويفسق

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam reports that mosques were sprinkled and swept in the Prophet’s time.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج ابن أبي شيبة عن زيد ابن أسلم قال : كان المسجد يرش ويقم على عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: يعقوب بن زيد
rows.claim: Yaqub ibn Zayd reports that the Prophet removed mosque dust with a palm frond.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عن يعقوب بن زيد أن النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام كان يتبع غبار المسجد بجريدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mosque members may furnish a mosque with brick, mats, or lamps from their own money, not mosque funds unless the ruler authorizes it, except where the endower specified this use.
rows.anchor: ولأهل المسجد أن يفرشوا المسجد بالآجر والحصير ويعلقوا القناديل لكن من مال أنفسهم لا من مال المسجد إلا بأمر الحاكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lavish lighting on set nights that draws children and idlers into noise and disrespect is a reprehensible innovation; patterned carpets that distract worshippers and diminish concentration should likewise be avoided.
rows.anchor: إيقاد القناديل الكثيرة فيها في ليالي معروفة من السنة كليلة السابع والعشرين من رمضان الموجب لاجتماع الصبيان وأهل البطالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some authorities recommend entering with the right foot, leaving with the left, and praying two rakahs before sitting when entering for a purpose other than prayer.
rows.anchor: ومن التعظيم أيضا تقديم الرجل اليمنى عند دخولها واليسرى عند الخروج منها وصلاة الداخل ركعتين قبل الجلوس إذا كان دخوله لغير الصلاة

rows.speaker: أبو قتادة
rows.claim: Abu Qatada reports the Prophet’s instruction to give mosques their due, explaining that this means praying two rakahs before sitting.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي شيبة عن أبي قتادة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : اعطوا المساجد حقها قيل : وما حقها قال : ركعتان قبل أن تسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mosques may be built high, unlike ordinary houses, but should not be decorated in ways that distract worshippers.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك أيضا بناؤها رفيعة عالية لا كسائر البيوت لكن لا ينبغي تزيينها بما يشوش على المصلين

rows.speaker: جبير بن مطعم
rows.claim: A report from Jubayr ibn Mutim says mosques should not be built with images or adorned with glass.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أخرجه ابن ماجه والطبراني عن جبير بن مطعم مرفوعا أنها لا تبنى بالتصاوير ولا تزين بالقوارير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret raising as constructing high buildings, citing Abraham’s raising the foundations of the House; al-Alusi prefers honoring the mosques generally, with lofty construction included among its instances.
rows.anchor: وفسر بعضهم الرفع ببنائها رفيعة كما في قوله تعالى : ( وإذ يرفع إبراهيم القواعد من البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestions that raising means needs being presented to God there or voices being raised in remembrance are unsound.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ترفع الأصوات بذكر الله عز وجل فيها ولا يخفى ما فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God’s command permission hints that the person being commanded is already inclined to the commanded act, as though seeking permission to carry it out.
rows.anchor: إلى المأمور به قبل الأمر به ناويا لتحقيقه كأنه مستأذن في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remembrance of God includes all forms of remembrance and religious learning; Ibn Abbas narrows it to monotheism or Qur’an recitation, and another view takes it as God’s beautiful names.
rows.anchor: والمراد بذكر اسمه تعالى شأنه ما يعم جميع أذكاره تعالى وجعل من ذلك المباحث العلمية المتعلقة به عز وجل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to interpret remembrance as affirming divine unity, specifically saying “There is no god but God.”
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما المراد به توحيده عز وجل وهو قول :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbih means declaring God transcendent and holy; it is used with or without the preposition li, as in “Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.”
rows.anchor: والتسبيح التنزيه والتقديس ويستعمل باللام وبدونها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن والضحاك
rows.claim: Tasbih may mean its ordinary sense or prayer, since prayer contains glorification; Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Dahhak report the prayer interpretation, and Ibn Abbas says every Qur’anic tasbih means prayer.
rows.anchor: وروي هذا عن ابن عباس والحسن والضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The specified times support reading tasbih as prayer; dawn and evening are singled out as especially honored and as common times of work and occupation.
rows.anchor: وأيد إرادة الصلاة هنا تعيين الأوقات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghuduww can be the plural of ghada or a verbal noun used for the time; al-asal is the plural of asil, though that plural pattern is not regular, while al-asl is another analysis for evening.
rows.anchor: والغدو جمع غداة كفتى وفتاة أو مصدر أطلق على الوقت الغدو

rows.speaker: مجلز
rows.claim: Mujliz reads al-īsāl as a verbal noun meaning entering the time of evening.
rows.anchor: بأن مجلز قرأ ( والأيصال ) مصدرا أي الدخول في وقت الأصيل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari analyzes al-asal as the plural of asl, like neck and necks; evening extends from the sun’s decline to morning, while the two terms can also mean the beginning and end of day.
rows.anchor: واختار الزمخشري أنه جمه أصل كعنق وأعناق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes al-ghadah to mean forenoon and says the forenoon prayer is mentioned in the Qur’an, reciting this verse through al-asal as evidence.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنه حمل الغداة على وقت الضحى وهو مقتضى ما أخرج ابن أبي شيبة والبيهقي في شعب الإيمان عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو بكر والبحتري عن حفص ومحبوب عن أبي عمرو والمنهال عن يعقوب والمفضل وأبان
rows.claim: These readers have yusabbahu in the masculine passive; its deputy subject may be lahu, fīhā, or bi-l-ghuduww, with the first preferred as nearest to the verb and a true attribution.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وأبو بكر والبحتري عن حفص ومحبوب عن أبي عمرو والمنهال عن يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the masculine passive reading, rijāl is raised either as the subject of an omitted verb or as the predicate of an omitted subject, supplying the men who glorify God.
rows.anchor: ورفع ( رجال ) على هذه القراءة على أنه فاعل لفعل محذوف

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة وابن وثاب
rows.claim: Abu Haywa and Ibn Waththab read tasbaḥu in the feminine active, with rijāl as its subject; the feminine agreement is licensed by the broken plural’s frequent feminine treatment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة وابن وثاب ( تسبح ) بالتاء الفوقية والبناء للفاعل

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jafar reads tasbaḥu in the feminine passive, taking the times as deputy subject with an extra bāʾ and figurative attribution; Abu Hayyan instead allows an implied tasbiḥa as subject, a reading al-Alusi’s cited authority prefers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر ( تسبح ) بالتاء الفوقية والبناء للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic example illustrates the accepted ellipsis of a verb or subject in this construction; many grammarians allow such ellipsis by analogy, unlike the explicitly disallowed use of an agent as a specification after a passive verb.
rows.anchor: وهذا نظير قوله : لبيك يزيد ضارع لخصومة ومختبط مما تطيح الطوائح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also interprets remembrance as recitation of God’s Book.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا المراد تلاوة كتابه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God is coordinated with raising the houses as a specific instance of the general honoring of mosques, not as an explanatory apposition.
rows.anchor: وعطف الذكر على الرفع من قبيل عطف الخاص على العام فإن ذكر اسمه تعالى فيها من أنواع تعظيمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause describing what does not distract them qualifies rijāl and reinforces the grandeur conveyed by its indefinite form, emphasizing their unbroken devotion despite every possible diversion.
rows.anchor: وقوله سبحانه : ( لا تلهيهم تجارة ( صفة له مؤكدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the reading discussed above, rijāl is raised as subject or predicate; its tanwin in every reading conveys magnificence.
rows.anchor: فرفع ( رجال ) على هذه القراءة على الفاعلية أو الخبرية كما سمعت آنفا والتنوين فيه على جميع القراءات للتفخيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Men are specified because they are especially suited to frequent mosques; a report from Umm Salama says women’s best mosques are the innermost parts of their homes.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص الرجال بالذكر لأنهم الأحقاء بالمساجد فقد أخرج أحمد والبيهقي عن أم سلمة عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم خير مساجد النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trade means exchange generally, while sale is one particular kind; sale is singled out because its profit is immediate and certain, unlike the uncertain future gain of other trade, so negating trade alone would not clearly negate its distraction.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص التجارة التي هي المعارضة مطلقا بذلك لكونها أقوى الصوارف عندهم وأشهرها أي لا يشغلهم نوع من أنواع التجارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating lā after trade emphasizes the negation; alternatively trade may mean profitable exchange and sale all exchange generally, making the second phrase a generalization after specification.
rows.anchor: وإفراده بالذكر اندراجه تحت التجارة للإيذان بإنافته على سائر أنواعها لأن ربحه متيقن ناجز وربح ما عداه متوقع

rows.speaker: الواقدي
rows.claim: Al-Waqidi says trade here means buying, its origin and starting point, which removes the need to construe trade and sale as different categories.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن الواقدي أن المراد بالتجارة هو الشراء لأنه أصلها ومبدؤها فلا تخصيص ولا تعميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes trade as importing goods, since bringing them in is customary to it; a report describing the men as traveling the earth to seek God’s bounty supports this.
rows.anchor: بالتجارة الجلب لأنه الغالب فيها فهو لازم لها عادة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra says the men described in the verse travel the land seeking God’s bounty; al-Dailami transmits a similar report from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد هذا ما أخرجه ابن أبي حاتم وابن مردويه عن أبي هريرة عن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they really were merchants, yet trade and sale never distracted them from remembrance; al-Dahhak shares this view, which al-Alusi regards as supported by the verse’s apparent wording.
rows.anchor: وروي ذلك عن ابن عباس + أخرج الطبراني وابن مردويه عنه أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative says the men had no trade or sale, so neither distracted them, and identifies them as people disengaged from worldly life such as the People of the Bench; al-Alusi prefers the merchant reading and says no reliable or weak report establishes this occasion.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنهم لم يكونوا تجارا والنفي راجع للقيد والمقيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God includes glorification, praise, and similar devotional acts.
rows.anchor: عن ذكر الله ( بالتسبيح والتحميد ونحوهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Establishing prayer means performing it at its appointed times without delay; the verbal noun iqāma is explained through deletion and vowel transfer from an original form.
rows.anchor: إقام الصلاة ( أي إقامتها لمواقيتها من غير تأخير

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains iqāma by changing wāw to alif and deleting an alif when two meet; al-Alusi objects that the change lacks its required condition.
rows.anchor: وعن الزجاج أنه قلبت الواو ألفا ثم حذف لاجتماع ألفين وأورد عليه أنه لا داعي إلى قلبها ألفا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra permits deleting the final alif either with compensatory tāʾ, as in iqāma, or through annexation, as in this verse; Sībawayh permits deletion without either compensation.
rows.anchor: تعويض التاء فيقال : إقامة أو الإضافة كما هنا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh allows the deletion without a compensatory tāʾ or annexation; the cited line is also explained by Khalid ibn Kulthum as using ʿadā for the plural of ʿadwa, meaning sides.
rows.anchor: ومذهب سيبويه جواز الحذف من غير تعويض التاء أو الإضافة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets zakat here as the wealth mandated for distribution to eligible recipients, a reading supported by the phrase’s construction as giving zakat.
rows.anchor: أي المال الذي فرض إخراجه للمستحقين كما روي عن الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets giving zakat as sincere obedience to God, but al-Alusi considers this interpretation remote.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما تفسير إيتاء الزكاة بإخلاص طاعة الله تعالى وفيه بعد كما ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakat is mentioned even though it is not performed in mosques because it commonly accompanies prayer and shows that the men’s good deeds are not limited to what they do in mosques.
rows.anchor: وإيراد هذا الفعل ههنا وإن لم يكن مما يفعل في البيوت لكونه قرينة لا تفارق إقامة الصلاة في عامة المواضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fear clause can further describe the men, be circumstantial to the object of “distract,” or stand independently as its explanation; in any case their fear is not confined to mosque settings.
rows.anchor: صفة أخرى لرجال أو حال من مفعول ( لا تلهيهم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm is the object of “they fear,” with an implied “punishment” or “terror” if supplied; making it a time adverb with an omitted object is remote, and making it an adverb of fear is untenable because they fear in this life.
rows.anchor: يوما ( مفعول ليخافون على تقدير مضاف أي عقاب يوم وهوله أو بدونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day is Judgment Day; the turning of hearts and eyes can mean that they themselves are convulsed and changed by terror, as in the description of the Confederates’ distress.
rows.anchor: والمراد به يوم القيامة ومعنى تقلب القلوب والأبصار فيه اضطرابها وتغيرها أنفسها فيه من الهول والفزع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations are that hearts understand what they did not and eyes see what they did not, or that hearts alternate between hope and fear while eyes look in every direction as people await their fate and books.
rows.anchor: أو تغير أحوالها بأن تفقه القلوب ما لم تكن تفقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that hearts and eyes turn over the embers of Hell, and al-Jubbaʾi’s account of successive fiery states, are rejected as unsound.
rows.anchor: ومثله قول الجبائي : أن المراد تنقل من حال إلى حال

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin reads the second tāʾ of tattaqalabu with sukūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن ( تتقلب ) بإسكان التاء الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone possesses the sovereign dominion of heaven and earth and all within them, entailing complete power and disposal over creation, destruction, life, death, commands, and prohibitions according to wise will.
rows.anchor: أي له سبحانه خاصة دون غيره لا استقلالا ولا اشتراكا السلطان القاهر والاستيلاء الباهر عليهما المستلزم للقدرة التامة والتصرف الكلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative may be nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, an adjective, explanatory apposition, or a substitute for the earlier relative; it may also be nominative or accusative as praise.
rows.anchor: ومحل الموصول الرفع على أنه خبر لمبتدأ محذوف والجملة مستانفة مقررة لما قبلها أو على أنه نعت للموصول أو بيان له أو بدل منه

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi prefers a nominative substitute because the relative clause was not known to the adversaries and thus explains the earlier relative; al-Alusi calls this far-fetched.
rows.anchor: واختار الطيبي أن محله الرفع على الإبدال وعلله بقوله لأن من حق الصلة أن تكون معلومة عند المخاطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has not assigned anyone the status of a child; alternatively, He has no child, contrary to claims about Christ, Ezra, or angels.
rows.anchor: أي لم ينزل أحدا منزلة الولد وقيل أي لم يكن ولد كما يزعم الذين يقولون في حق المسيح وعزير والملائكة

words: وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ شَرِيكٌۭ فِى ٱلْمُلْكِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial of a partner expressly refutes dualists who posit multiple gods, although God’s exclusive ownership already entails that there is no partner.
rows.anchor: وأفرد بالذكر مع أن ما ذكر من اختصاص ملكهما به تعالى مستلزم له قطعا للتصريح ببطلان زعم الثنوية القائلين بتعدد الآلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial of a child is placed between exclusive ownership and denial of a partner to assert its independent force and prevent it from seeming a continuation of the first clause.
rows.anchor: وتوسيط نفي اتخاذ الولد بينهما للتنبيه على استقلاله وأصالته والاحتراز عن توهم كونه تتمة للأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God brought everything into existence in measured, proportionate form according to His wise will, as with the human being’s particular materials, forms, and shapes.
rows.anchor: أي أحدثه إحداثا جاريا على سنن التقدير والتسوية حسبما اقتضته إرادته المبنية على الحكم البالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God equipped each created thing with the properties and actions suited to its purpose; for humans these include understanding, reflection, livelihood, crafts, and varied work.
rows.anchor: فقدره ( أي هيأه لما أراد به من الخصائص والأفعال اللائقة به

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj’s preferred reading distinguishes creation as proportioning from تقدير as preparing for purpose, so the wording is not repetitive; alternatively creation means bringing into existence and explicit تقدير separately marks the measured manner of each creation.
rows.anchor: فلا تكرار في الآية لما ظهر من أن التقدير الدال عليه الخلق بمعنى التسوية والمعبر عنه بلفظه بمعنى التهيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the second تقدير as assigning each thing its lifespan and sustaining it until its appointed term.
rows.anchor: وقيل التقدير الثاني هو التقدير للبقاء إلى الأجل المسمى فكأنه قيل وأوجد كل شيء على سنن التقدير فأدامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed inversion in the wording does not remove the apparent repetition unless one of the preceding explanations is adopted.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن في الكلام قلبا وهو على ما فيه لا يدفع لزوم التكرار بدون أحد الأوجه المذكورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Universal creation refutes dualists who assign evil and good to different creators, and is also directed against the Muʿtazilite account of voluntary creaturely acts.
rows.anchor: وفيها رد على الثنوية القائلين بأن خالق الشر غير خالف الخير ولا يضر كونه معلوما مما تقدم

rows.speaker: إرشاد العقل السليم
rows.claim: The clause explains the preceding denials: since God created all things, everything else lies under His dominion, so none can be His child or partner.
rows.anchor: أنها جارية مجرى العليل لما قبلها من الجمل المنتظمة في سلك الصلة

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi views exclusive ownership as a prelude to denying child and partner, then creation as a further reason that God’s status as originator and owner precludes both; the text links this to the denial of a child in 6:101.
rows.anchor: وذكر الطيبي أن قوله تعالى : ( له ملك السماوات والأرض )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi adds that creation may state explicitly what was already implicit, intensifying the condemnation of the polytheists in the following cited verse.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال : إن هذه الجملة تصريح بما علم قبل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the disbelievers as the polytheists already mentioned; they are called disbelievers to condemn them and signal the cause of their objection. Another view identifies a group of Jews.
rows.anchor: والمراد بهم المشركون كما صح عن ابن عباس وهم القائلون أولا والتعبير عنهم بعنوان الكفر لذمهم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their challenge means, “Why was the Qur’an not revealed to him all at once?” The wording can mean revelation as a report, with no gradual delivery intended.
rows.anchor: أي أنزل عليه كخبر بمعنى أخبر فلا قصد فيه إلى التدريج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “All at once” is a circumstantial accusative, and wāḥidah is an emphatic adjective; reading the challenge as asking for a single collective division would contradict the demand for one whole.
rows.anchor: فإنه لو قصد ذلك لتدافعا إذ يكون المعنى لولا فرق القرآن جملة واحدة والتفريق ينافي الجملية

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Hadiths and early reports indicate that the Torah, Gospel, and Psalms were revealed all at once; al-Suyuti says this was nearly consensus, rejecting Ibn al-Kamal’s claim that the Torah came gradually over eighteen years.
rows.anchor: كما أنزلت التوراة والانجيل والزبور على ما تدل عليه الأحاديث والآثار حتى كاد يكون اجماعا كما قال السيوطي

rows.speaker: ابن الكمال
rows.claim: Ibn al-Kamal argues that the Torah was revealed in stages over eighteen years, citing its own texts; al-Alusi says no decisive Qur’anic or Prophetic proof supports the contrary and attributes the claim to incomplete research.
rows.anchor: فتقول ابن الكمال إن التوراة أنزلت منجمة في ثماني عشرة سنة ويدل عليه نصوص التوراة ولا قاطع بخلافه من الكتاب والسنة

words: لَوْلَا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ جُمْلَةًۭ وَٰحِدَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection has little force: the Qur’an’s inimitability is unaffected by whole or gradual revelation, and gradual delivery has benefits that the verse itself proceeds to explain.
rows.anchor: وهذا الاعتراض مما لا طائل تحته لأن الاعجاز مما لا يختلف بنزوله جملة أو مفرقا مع أن للتفريق فوائد منها ما ذكره الله تعالى بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One argument says the Qur’an’s truth is proven by its inimitable eloquence, which matches each passage to its circumstances, a match said to be impossible if it came all at once; al-Alusi contests that premise in the next segment.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن شاهد صحة القرآن اعجازه وذلك ببلاغته وهي بمطابقته لمقتضى الحال

words: لَوْلَا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ جُمْلَةًۭ وَٰحِدَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi denies that eloquence matching circumstances requires gradual revelation: a single revelation could match each passage to later events; the Qur’an did descend all at once to the lowest heaven, which would otherwise imply a non-inimitable portion, and this may heighten its miracle.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن قوله : ولا يتيسر الخ منوع فانه يجوز أن ينزل دفعة واحدة مع رعاية المطابقة المذكورة في كل جملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause is God’s reply to the objection, explaining one wisdom in gradual revelation; kādhālika is an adverbial description of the implied revelation, or may be circumstantial.
rows.anchor: كذلك لنثبت به فؤادك استئناف وارد من جهته تعالى لرد مقالتهم وبيان بعض الحكم في تنزيله تدريجيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual revelation strengthened the Prophet’s heart by easing memorization, understanding, and precise retention, showing successive wisdoms, repeatedly bringing Gabriel, and renewing the challenge to critics with each passage.
rows.anchor: فان في تنزيله مفرقا تيسيرا لحفظ النظم وفهم المعاني وضبط الكلام والوقوف على تفاصيل ما روعي فيه من الحكم والمصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further benefits of gradual revelation include distinguishing later abrogating verses from earlier abrogated ones and combining situational clues with verbal evidence to recognize eloquence suited to context.
rows.anchor: منها معرفة الناسخ المتأخر نزوله من المنسوخ المتقدم نزوله المخالف لحكمه ومنها انضمام القرائن الحالية إلى الدلالات اللفظية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative makes kādhālika part of the disbelievers’ statement, with the comparison describing the Qur’an or the manner of its revelation and referring to the earlier scriptures.
rows.anchor: وقيل : قووله تعالى ( كذلك ) من تمام كلام الكفرة والكاف نصب على الحال من القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim calls the lām an oath particle, reconstructing “By God, We shall surely establish”; al-Alusi, citing Abu Hayyan, calls this extremely weak and rejects the related Akhfash analysis.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حاتم : هي لام القسم والتقدير والله لنثبتن

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abd Allah reads liyuthabbit, with yāʾ, meaning “so that God may make firm.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله ليثبت بالياء أي ليثبت الله تعالى
